rich_summary: This section recounts the story of the ascetic Jajali, whose extreme stillness during penance allows a pair of birds to build a nest and raise their young on his head. Out of compassion he refuses to move for months, protecting the eggs and chicks until they finally fly away. Believing this patience proves his spiritual greatness, Jajali becomes proud and proclaims his merit. An unseen voice rebukes him, saying he is not equal in righteousness to Tuladhara, a humble merchant of Benares. Jajali seeks him out and questions how a trader could possess such wisdom. Tuladhara replies that true morality is universal friendliness and harmlessness toward all beings, practiced in thought, word, and deed. He argues that compassion and non‑injury surpass ritual austerities and even common professions may hide subtle violence, reframing righteousness as ethical living rather than ascetic pride.

top_scenes.scene_text: An unmoving ascetic stands like a wooden post in the forest while two small birds build a grass nest in his matted hair atop his head.
The grown fledglings spread their wings and fly away from the nest on the sage’s head as he finally opens his eyes with quiet pride.
In a busy market at Benares, the humble merchant Tuladhara stands beside balanced scales greeting the austere sage Jajali who has come to challenge him.
